newsitem.title: USA: Industry blames gasoline prices on low oil supply.
newsitem.headline: Industry blames gasoline prices on low oil supply.

text.p: The U.S. oil industry Wednesday said gasoline prices were high because crude oil supplies had failed to keep up with demand, and not because stocks of refined products had been low in the last 18 months.
"Worldwide supply of crude has not kept up with increased demand," said Edward Murphy, director of statistics for the American Petroleum Institute.
"It's the crude oil price increases that are driving up the gasoline prices," he said at a news conference.
High gasoline prices last summer and soaring heating oil prices this winter spurred consumer groups to press the government to make oil companies beef up their inventories.
But Murphy said if oil companies had put more product into storage instead of selling it, people would have had to pay even more for gasoline and heating oil as consumption rose.
"The inventory drawdown was one that was necessitated by an imbalance between demand and supply," he said.
U.S. petroleum demand grew by 2.8 percent to 19.2 million barrels in 1996 from 1995, compared with average demand growth of 1.5 percent over the previous three years.
Total petroleum supply in 1996 was 19.1 million bpd, up 3.6 percent from 1995, including a 6 percent increase in imports of crude and products to 9.4 million bpd, API said.
Last summer consumer groups and lawmakers blamed the oil companies for adopting a policy of keeping lean inventories, which drove prices higher as demand soared.
But repeating what API said last summer, Murphy said stocks over the last 18 months did not indicate a trend toward low inventories.

According to industry data, oil companies held 1 billion to 1.1 billion in petroleum inventories from 1986 to 1995. But in mid-1995 and 1996, stock levels dropped to between 900 and 975 million barrels.
"I don't think we can look at what happened in the last 18 months and say this is a change in inventory behavior," Murphy said.

Gasoline futures prices last year jumped from a low of 51.5 cents a gallon in February to a five-year high of 78.1 cents by the end of April. Prices eased by 20 cents by the end of June. However they have risen steadily since then to about 72 cents a gallon.
Gasoline stocks at the end of December at 194.8 million barrels were down 3.7 percent from December 1995, prompting fears among consumer groups that prices could spike again this summer.
